name: Lennar Corporation

profile.description: Lennar, founded in 1954 and based in Miami, is one of the two largest U.S. homebuilders. It builds single-family homes for first-time, move-up, active-adult, and luxury buyers across its East, Central, Texas, and West segments, and it also runs mortgage, title, multifamily, and strategic technology-investment businesses. In fiscal Q3 2026 (ended August 31) it delivered 20,840 homes on $8.05B of revenue (-9% YoY), with home-sale gross margin compressed to 15.8%, and it cut its FY2026 delivery target to 80,000-81,000 homes. Stuart Miller has been sole CEO since co-CEO Jon Jaffe retired at the end of 2025. Market cap is about $21.7B.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Lennar has run a technology-investment arm whose portfolio still affects earnings, including a $53M mark-to-market loss in Q3 FY2026, and it has scaled solar-equipped homes to about 13,000 [1][7]. These extend the core homebuilding model rather than open a major new revenue stream. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI products or quantified AI savings were found, and employees describe chaotic technology-leadership turnover, with major disruption at each CTO change [4]. Market Share (2/2): Lennar is one of the two largest U.S. builders, with FY2026 deliveries guided to 80,000-81,000 homes and 20,840 delivered in Q3 alone [1][2]. Product Pipeline (0/2): No new product lines with launch timelines. Guidance covers delivery volumes and margins only [2]. R&D Intensity (0/1): No disclosed R&D [3].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Lennar's focus on delivering quality, affordable homes, with an everything's-included feature approach, is clear about what it does and for whom but is not distinctive among large builders [7]. Community Impact (1/2): The company publishes social-responsibility reports covering community and sustainability initiatives, including about 13,000 solar-powered homes [7]. However, shareholder proponents in 2024 and 2025 said it lacks a climate transition plan, and Sustainalytics ranks it 82 of 83 homebuilders on ESG risk [6]. Employee Retention (0/2): Glassdoor shows 3.4 stars, 52% recommend-to-a-friend, and 60% CEO approval, with reviews citing constant strategy shifts and frequent leadership changes [4]. Insider Buying (0/2): No meaningful net insider buying was identified in the last 12 months.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Scored mechanically as a Dividend stock (2.2% yield, dividends paid every year since at least 1984). D/E is 19.9% (1.0) [3]. TTM ROE is 6.0% (0.40) and TTM net margin 4.1% (0.21) as gross margins compressed [3]. TTM revenue fell 8.0% YoY to $32.0B (0.40), while 5-year revenue per share grew about 12.8% annually (82% cumulative), flattered by buybacks (1.0) [3]. Forward P/E of about 18.0x is derived from FY2027 consensus EPS of $5.05 (1.0). The payout ratio is 37.6% (1.0). Dividends have been paid for 42 consecutive years (1.0, 2x), but the $0.50 quarterly payout has been flat since 2024, so consecutive years of growth is 0 (0). The 5-year dividend CAGR is about 14.9%, from $1.00 to $2.00 annually (1.0, 2x) [5]. Weighted sum 9.01/12 gives 7.5, which rounds to 8. The liquidity floor is easily passed at about $373M per day.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Building homes means buying land, developing it, and managing trades on job sites, all physical and permit-bound work that AI cannot substitute [1]. AI-enabled digital mortgage and title competitors could pressure Lennar's ancillary financial-services margins at the edges, but analysts do not cite AI as a risk to homebuilding economics, which turn on mortgage rates and affordability [2]. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI revenue. The technology-investment portfolio produced a $53M mark-to-market loss in Q3 FY2026 [2].

infinite_game.summary: Lennar has endured for more than 70 years under the Miller family, a continuity Sinek respects. Its operating philosophy, however, is volume-driven: it keeps production steady and sells through incentives, accepting gross margin falling to 15.8%, and its competitive identity is about scale and efficiency rather than a cause. Employee reviews describing chaotic strategy shifts and technology-leadership churn suggest a weak Circle of Safety. Sinek would see a durable finite competitor rather than a cause-driven infinite player.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Delivering affordable, quality homes is service-oriented, but Lennar frames it as an operating strategy of volume, pace, and efficiency rather than a vision people sacrifice for. The climate-transition criticism suggests the purpose does not extend to long-horizon stewardship [6][7].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Management has held its even-flow production strategy and kept investing in technology through a high-rate downturn, absorbing margin compression and mark-to-market losses rather than cutting volume for near-term earnings [1][2].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Top leadership is very stable, with Stuart Miller in long-tenured leadership and an orderly hand-off when co-CEO Jon Jaffe retired at the end of 2025 [4]. A 3.4 Glassdoor rating with reviews of constant change executed chaotically keeps the score from reaching high trust [4].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Lennar has expanded beyond homebuilding into multifamily development, financial services, and technology investing [3][7]. These are adjacent extensions rather than a reinvention of the core business.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Competitive positioning against D.R. Horton and others centers on volume, pace, and pricing incentives. A shareholder proponent contrasted Lennar unfavorably with KB Home's all-electric progress without evident management engagement [6].

investment_thesis: Lennar is a scale leader trading near book value: 1.0x P/B, about 18x FY2027 consensus EPS of $5.05, D/E of only 19.9%, and 42 years of uninterrupted dividends with a 37.6% payout [3][5]. Q4 FY2026 guidance of 22,000-23,000 deliveries and home-sale gross margin of 15.5-16.0% points to stabilization, and consensus expects EPS to grow from about $4.82 in FY2026 to $6.19 in FY2028 as rates ease [2][3]. The Inspire score of 39 (ALIGNED, including Product Access and Affordability) supports faith-based allocation.
thesis_continued: The bear case is a housing downturn that has not bottomed. Q3 FY2026 revenue fell 9%, net earnings fell 52% to $284M, new orders fell 9%, home-sale gross margin dropped to 15.8% from 17.5%, and EPS of $1.19 GAAP ($1.23 adjusted) missed the $1.29 consensus [1][2]. With mortgage rates around 6.8% and rising, management cut FY2026 deliveries to 80,000-81,000, and the volume-over-margin strategy keeps TTM ROE at only 6.0% [2][3]. The dividend has been flat at $0.50 per quarter since 2024, and a Sustainalytics ranking of 82 of 83 homebuilders on ESG risk is a governance flag [5][6].
key_catalysts: Mortgage-rate relief below 6.5% lifting orders and reducing the incentives that compress home-sale margins [2]
Q4 FY2026 delivery of 22,000-23,000 homes at 15.5-16.0% gross margin, showing margin stabilization [2]
Continued buybacks, with the diluted share count falling from about 256M to 238M YoY, and potential dividend growth resuming [3]
key_risks: Mortgage rates near or above 6.8% further eroding affordability and orders, which fell 9% YoY in Q3 [2]
Gross-margin compression from heavy incentives, with home-sale margin at 15.8% versus 17.5% a year ago and Q4 guided to 15.5-16.0% [2]
Technology-investment mark-to-market losses ($53M in Q3) and execution risk from frequent strategy and leadership changes [2][4]
